title: Reading Paul: Romans

objectives.can: Follow a Pauline argument: γάρ and οὖν, rhetorical questions, μὴ γένοιτο, long conditional and causal chains.

explanation.summary: Romans is an argument, and the way to read it is to follow the small words that carry the argument: γάρ, οὖν, δέ, ἀλλά, and the phrases that answer an objection. This lesson names those signals and then sends you into Romans 5:1–11.

sections.heading: γάρ and οὖν: reason and conclusion
body: Two connectives do most of the work of Paul's argument. γάρ, 'for', gives a reason or an explanation for what has just been said. οὖν, 'so, then', draws a conclusion or resumes the argument. Both stand in second place in their clause, after the first word or phrase.

In Romans 5:1 the sentence opens Δικαιωθέντες οὖν, 'having been justified, then', and the οὖν draws a consequence from the argument before it. In 5:6–8 the verses chain with γάρ and δέ: Ἔτι γὰρ in 5:6, μόλις γάρ in 5:7, and ὑπὲρ γὰρ in the same verse. Each γάρ explains the one before it, so the verses are read as a line of support, not as separate statements.
Always ask of a γάρ: what is it giving the reason for? And of an οὖν: what conclusion is it drawing, and from what?

sections.heading: Chains, 'not only … but also', and 'much more'
body: Paul likes to build a sentence out of links. In 5:3–4 each noun is the result of the one before: ἡ θλῖψις ὑπομονὴν κατεργάζεται, then ἡ δὲ ὑπομονὴ δοκιμήν, then ἡ δὲ δοκιμὴ ἐλπίδα. The verb κατεργάζεται is stated once in 5:3 and understood in the two clauses that follow, each opened by ἡ δέ.

The elliptical formula οὐ μόνον δέ, ἀλλὰ καί, 'and not only that, but also', occurs in 5:3 and again in 5:11. It carries the thought on without a verb of its own; the verb or participle comes after καί (καυχώμεθα in 5:3, καυχώμενοι in 5:11).

A form of argument that grammarians and commentators often point out is the 'much more' argument. In 5:9 and 5:10, πολλῷ μᾶλλον ('much more') draws a conclusion from a point already granted. In 5:10, εἰ γάρ … κατηλλάγημεν gives the starting point as given, and πολλῷ μᾶλλον … σωθησόμεθα draws from it the greater certainty of what follows. Notice the participle phrases that surround the verbs: ἐχθροὶ ὄντες, 'while being enemies', and καταλλαγέντες, 'having been reconciled'.

sections.heading: Genitive absolutes and long sentences
body: Romans 5:6 and 5:8 both contain a genitive absolute built on ὄντων ἡμῶν: ὄντων ἡμῶν ἀσθενῶν, 'while we were weak', and ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν, 'while we were sinners'. The genitive pair is a circumstance, set apart from the main clause: Christ died while we were in that state.

A long sentence of Paul's is usually a series of such pieces: participles, ὅτι clauses, prepositional phrases with διά. Find the main verb first, then see how each piece is attached. Not every piece belongs to the main verb; some belong to a participle, and some to a noun.

sections.heading: Questions and μὴ γένοιτο
body: Paul often argues by raising an objection as a question and answering it at once. Romans 6:1 asks Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; and then puts a possible wrong conclusion: ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ; The verb ἐπιμένωμεν is a subjunctive, used in a question about what 'we' should do.

The answer comes in 6:2: μὴ γένοιτο, 'by no means'. γένοιτο is an optative, literally 'may it not happen', and grammarians call this use an optative of wish that has become a fixed way of rejecting a conclusion. After it Paul gives his reason (6:2 continues with οἵτινες … πῶς ἔτι ζήσομεν;). The same pattern recurs in 6:15.

sections.heading: Some words Paul uses a great deal
body: Certain nouns come back again and again in Romans. Give each a range of senses, and let the context choose. The table gives a range of ordinary uses in the New Testament; scholars debate which sense fits some verses, and the table does not settle those debates.
Watch the cases and prepositions. The same noun means something slightly different after κατά, ἐν, ἐκ, διά or ὑπό.

head: Word
Range of senses
Where to see it
rows: justice, uprightness in conduct, a right standing; the noun is related to the verb δικαιόω, found in 5:1
trust, faith, faithfulness, what is believed, a pledge
law, a rule, custom; the law of Moses; a principle
flesh, the body, a human being, human nature in its weakness
wind, breath, a spirit, the Spirit, a disposition

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read Romans 5:1–11 as a single movement. The first sentence says what follows from being justified (οὖν); 5:3–5 builds the chain of suffering and hope; 5:6–8 gives the grounds with γάρ and δέ; and 5:9–11 argues 'much more' from what has been done to what is sure. Read it twice: first following only the connectives, then phrase by phrase.

misunderstandings: Translating every γάρ as 'for' without asking what it explains. It may explain only the clause just before it, or the whole earlier argument.
Reading οὖν as always 'therefore'. It can also resume the argument after an aside.
Taking μὴ γένοιτο as a general wish. In Paul it is the rejection of a conclusion raised by a question.
Treating the nouns in the table as having one fixed meaning each. The meaning is chosen from the context and the construction.

deeper.heading: Long sentences and the shape of Pauline argument
body: Readers have noticed that Paul dictated his letters and that his sentences sometimes break off, restart, or run on with participle after participle. Grammarians describe such sentences as anacolutha or as periods, depending on the case; the grammar describes the effect, but whether a particular break was intended is judged verse by verse, and readers differ.

practice.explain: The question is followed by the proposed conclusion, ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ; which Paul then rejects with μὴ γένοιτο in 6:2.

options: Each gives a reason or explanation for what has just been said
check.explain: γάρ means 'for'. In 5:7 it explains the claim of 5:6 by pointing to how rarely someone dies for a righteous person.

check.explain: ὁ θεός is the nominative; τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην is the accusative object. Χριστός is the subject of the verb inside the ὅτι clause, ἀπέθανεν.

check.prompt: What is the logic of πολλῷ οὖν μᾶλλον … σωθησόμεθα?

options: If this has already happened, the further result is all the more sure
The result is unrelated to what has happened
The result happened in the past
The further result is less sure than what has happened
check.explain: πολλῷ μᾶλλον means 'much more'. σωθησόμεθα is future passive, 'we shall be saved'; the participle δικαιωθέντες, 'having been justified', gives what has been done already.

check.prompt: How does ἐχθροὶ ὄντες (words 2–3) relate to κατηλλάγημεν?

options: It is unconnected to the verb
It gives the circumstance: while we were enemies we were reconciled
It is a command to the enemies
It gives the result: so that we were enemies
check.explain: ὄντες is a present participle of εἰμί agreeing with the subject of κατηλλάγημεν. The present participle describes the state at the time of the main verb.

check.prompt: What does μὴ γένοιτο (words 0–1) do in this verse?

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: It rejects the conclusion suggested in the question before it: by no means
It confirms the conclusion: let it happen
check.explain: γένοιτο is an optative; with μή it is the fixed form that Paul uses to refuse a wrong inference. The confirming answer would be a plain affirmative, not μὴ γένοιτο.

check.prompt: What does οὐ μόνον δέ, ἀλλὰ καί (words 0–4) say?

options: And not only that, but also …
Not only, so then not at all
check.explain: οὐ μόνον … ἀλλὰ καί is the common 'not only … but also' pattern. Here it has no verb of its own and the next word is the participle καυχώμενοι.

check.prompt: What is the job of the ὅτι clause that begins at word 5?

options: It gives the ground for the statement that hope does not disappoint
check.explain: Here ὅτι means 'because', giving the reason for ἡ ἐλπὶς οὐ καταισχύνει. The perfect ἐκκέχυται, 'has been poured out', states a result that stands.

check.prompt: What does εἰδότες ὅτι ἡ θλῖψις ὑπομονὴν κατεργάζεται (words 9–14) add?

quoted.title: Romans
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: The ground of the boasting: knowing that affliction produces endurance
A past event: affliction produced endurance once
check.explain: εἰδότες is a participle of οἶδα agreeing with the subject of καυχώμεθα; ὅτι introduces what is known. The present κατεργάζεται states a general truth.

reading.why: Eleven verses where οὖν opens the passage, γάρ chains the support, a verbless chain runs through 5:3–4, a genitive absolute appears twice, and πολλῷ μᾶλλον closes the argument.
